title: 21. Determining agreement between metabolizable energy intake values derived from wet-chemistry analysis and measured individual animal gas flux and performance.
content:
Abstract
Automated head chamber systems (AHCS; GreenFeed, C-Lock Inc., Rapid City, SD) can assess carbon dioxide, methane emissions, as well as oxygen consumption of cattle in their production environment. This opens the door to estimating heat production (HP) of unrestrained cattle. When HP is added to an estimate of recovered energy (RE), metabolizable energy (ME) intake (MEI) can be calculated. Previous research has demonstrated excellent agreement between AHCS – estimated MEI and MEI required for observed levels of growth performance. However, AHCS estimated MEI has not been compared with MEI estimated as actual dry matter intake (DMI) times ME concentration derived from wet chemistry analyses. Wet chemistry estimates of total digestible nutrients using summative equations can be converted to digestible energy (DE) by multiplying by 4.409. Digestible energy can then be used to estimate ME concentration. For this study, data was compiled from 3 previous trials that included beef steers [n = 99; initial shrunk body weight (SBW) = 256 to 640 kg and final SBW = 344 to 711 kg]. Cattle were fed diets that ranged from TDN. Emissions data were recorded by an AHCS, and individual intake was measured with precision feeding systems (PFS; SmartFeed Pro, C-Lock Inc., Rapid City, SD) or Calan head gates (American Calan, Northwood, NH). Three equations were used to estimate MEI (Mcal/d): MEI_NASEM (DE × 0.82 × DMI); MEI_Galyean [(0.9611 × DE – 0.2999) × DMI], and MEI_Hales [(DE – 0.39) × DMI]. Metabolizable energy intake was also estimated using the AHCS (MEI_AHCS) approach that summed estimates of HP from AHCS and RE from observed average daily gain and predicted empty body weight. Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) were used to assess precision between MEI_AHCS and the MEI values derived based on dietary wet chemistry. There was a significant positive correlation (P < 0.01) between MEI_AHCS with MEI_ NASEM (r = 0.80), MEI_Galyean (r = 0.80), and MEI_Hales (r = 0.80). Lin’s concordance correlation coefficients (CCC) were used to characterize the agreement (considering precision and accuracy) between methods, which is the product of r and a bias correction factor (Cb), which is analogous to a slope and mean bias. The MEI_Galyean (Cb = 0.98) and MEI_Hales (Cb = 0.99) had greater Cb with MEI_AHCS than MEI_NASEM (Cb = 0.88). Accordingly, MEI_AHCS had better agreement with MEI_Galyean (CCC = 0.79) and MEI_Hales (CCC = 0.80) compared with MEI_ NASEM (CCC = 0.71). The agreement between wet chemistry estimated MEI and MEI_AHCS methods provide further support for the concept of utilizing the AHCS in conducting energetic research of cattle in their natural environments. The MEI_Galyean and MEI_Hales estimates of MEI had similar precision but greater accuracy with MEI_AHCS than the MEI_NASEM, suggesting improvement by these updated equations.
